title: Update: Before And After In 1 Day, and The Prompt That Did It
author: bingewavecinema
selftext:
Yesterday I posted about the prompt system I put together to correctly develop a game with the least amount of future wasted tokens from missing basic and critical features.

* **The prompts:**[ https://github.com/Glitch-Gaming-Platform/AI-Prompts-For-Game-Development](https://github.com/Glitch-Gaming-Platform/AI-Prompts-For-Game-Development)
* **Game made from those prompts:**[ https://www.glitch.fun/games/9a698a9d-1b27-4c78-9256-0f458368737d/play](https://www.glitch.fun/games/9a698a9d-1b27-4c78-9256-0f458368737d/play)
* **Source code:**[ https://github.com/Glitch-Gaming-Platform/Glitch-Games-FarmRise-Tycoon](https://github.com/Glitch-Gaming-Platform/Glitch-Games-FarmRise-Tycoon)

Here is the prompt I used for improving the graphics:

>  
I want you game graphically and animations perfect. It should be utterly perfect, visually beautiful, with every single thing done at AAA quality from textures to physics to anything you could think of.

>Fan out sub-agents and have sub-agents tackle each one individually so that the game is utterly perfect. You should /loop on each item and have a separate sub-agent check it visually to ensure it looks triple A. That separate sub-agent should be a really harsh critic, and if it doesn't look triple A, it should keep going.

>Don't stop until each sub-agent is utterly wowed with the quality.  It should literally compare them side by side blind and say which one looks better.  Fan out sub-agents and ultracode.

  
There is a strong warning; this will burn your tokens. So if you are on the $20, you will probably have to wait until next week to complete.

Followin the prompt system, in 2 day you will have a playable core loop, desktop and mobile optimization, asset pipelines, performance optimization, collision detection, sound affects, music loops, visual affects, onboarding, user progression, saving and loading, menu system, ability to distribute on other platforms, built-in analytics, a full testing suite and extensive documentation. This allows a full prototype of a game and to start getting feedback.

replies.author: bingewavecinema
replies.body:
Normally yes, but this is why I wrote the prompt system for people to follow so they don't have these issues.

Notice how the game works on mobile? but isn't has high quality as desktop? that is because from the start it has two graphic systems installed to accommodate for different devices.

From the start you want your game to have:

* Low-poly assets follow strict triangle budgets.
* Shared materials and vertex colors reduce GPU work.
* Repeated objects use instancing to minimize draw calls.
* Graphics update only when game state changes.
* Particle effects use reusable fixed-size pools.
* Mobile devices use lower resolution and fewer effects.
* Only one light casts shadows.
* Assets and models load only when needed.
* Requests are cached and deduplicated.
* Compression and LODs are used only when profiling justifies them.

And then solving performance issues with higher quality graphics is much easier when its done at the start of the game.

comments.author: ItsAlwaysTerminal
comments.body:
This might be the dumbest fucking prompt I have ever seen. Your qualifiers arent actually qualifiers and you are using "AAA quality" as both a requirement and an acceptance test without any kind of measurable definition and the weights can swing wildly on this. There's a reason this is hammering out tokens. This isnt an ideal prompt  but these things should look more like:

# Mission: Transform the Existing Game Into an Exceptional, Production-Quality Experience

You are acting as the **Executive Game Director, Technical Director, Art Director, Animation Director, and QA Lead** for this repository.

Your assignment is not merely to make the game functional.

Your assignment is to systematically inspect, improve, validate, and polish the existing game until every player-facing aspect reaches the highest practical quality achievable within the project's technology, assets, performance envelope, and gameplay design.

The desired result is:

* immediately visually impressive
* aesthetically coherent
* technically polished
* responsive and satisfying to control
* richly animated
* physically convincing where appropriate
* free of obvious placeholder-quality presentation
* internally consistent in art direction
* performant
* stable
* visually legible during gameplay
* polished at both macro and micro levels

Treat mediocre output as a defect.

Do **not** interpret "AAA" as "add more effects."

AAA-level polish means deliberate composition, consistency, excellent motion, strong feedback, convincing materials, appropriate detail, robust technical execution, and the absence of obvious weak points.

# CORE OPERATING PRINCIPLE

Do not perform this task as one monolithic agent.

Act as the **coordinating director** and aggressively fan work out to specialist sub-agents.

Each major quality domain must have:

1. an implementation specialist,
2. an independent reviewer/critic,
3. an objective or semi-objective acceptance rubric,
4. visual or runtime evidence,
5. an iterative repair loop.

The agent that implements an area MUST NOT be the sole agent deciding whether that area is good enough.

Use independent adversarial review.

When parallel work is safe, parallelize aggressively.

When work touches overlapping systems or files, coordinate ownership and sequence the work to prevent agents from overwriting one another.

Use the strongest coding/reasoning mode available, including **ultracode** or its equivalent, for difficult implementation work.

Use `/loop`, iterative agent execution, or the closest available mechanism whenever repeated improvement is beneficial.

# DO NOT STOP AT "WORKS"

For every system, distinguish between these levels:

# Level 1 — Functional

The feature works.

This is NOT sufficient.

# Level 2 — Technically Sound

The implementation is robust, maintainable, performant, and free of obvious technical defects.

Still NOT sufficient.

# Level 3 — Visually / Experientially Good

It looks and feels professionally made.

Still not necessarily sufficient.

# Level 4 — Polished

Transitions, secondary motion, effects, timing, materials, composition, sound/visual feedback if applicable, and edge cases are refined.

# Level 5 — Independently Accepted

A separate critical agent attempts to find reasons the implementation is inferior, compares it against professional-quality references when possible, and cannot identify a materially valuable improvement that can reasonably be implemented.

Only Level 5 counts as complete.

# PHASE 0 — UNDERSTAND THE PROJECT BEFORE MODIFYING IT

Before changing code or assets, inspect the project comprehensively.

Determine:

* engine/framework
* renderer
* programming language
* asset pipeline
* directory structure
* existing graphics systems
* animation system
* physics system
* camera implementation
* lighting system
* shader/material architecture
* VFX system
* post-processing
* audio feedback systems if relevant
* UI/HUD
* game-state architecture
* performance characteristics
* existing automated tests
* existing screenshot or rendering tests
* current playable content
* intended gameplay loop
* existing art direction
* obvious placeholder assets
* known bugs
* build/run commands
* target platform(s)
* target resolution
* likely target hardware

Run the game.

Do not judge quality solely from source code.

Observe actual runtime output.

Capture baseline evidence:

* representative screenshots
* representative gameplay footage if supported
* FPS/frame-time measurements
* major scenes
* important gameplay states
* player movement
* interactions
* impacts
* transitions
* UI
* environmental motion
* camera behavior

Create a **Baseline Quality Report** before major modification.

# PHASE 1 — CREATE A QUALITY BACKLOG

Inspect the game as a highly critical professional game-review team.

Identify every material weakness you can find.

Do not restrict yourself to items explicitly mentioned in this prompt.

Create a prioritized backlog grouped into at least the following domains.

# A. ART DIRECTION AND VISUAL COHESION

Audit:

* overall visual identity
* shape language
* color palette
* contrast hierarchy
* environment composition
* focal points
* silhouette quality
* readability
* consistency between assets
* consistency between gameplay and UI
* environmental storytelling
* visual clutter
* obvious procedural or generic-looking elements
* areas that look like programmer art
* areas that look unfinished
* repetitive assets
* scale consistency
* proportion consistency

Determine what art direction the existing game is trying to achieve.

Do not randomly introduce incompatible visual styles.

Improve the game toward a coherent art direction.

# B. GEOMETRY AND ENVIRONMENT DETAIL

Audit:

* model quality
* silhouettes
* geometry density
* visible low-poly artifacts
* intersections
* floating objects
* gaps
* clipping
* repetitive geometry
* environment dressing
* terrain quality
* architectural detail
* props
* decal opportunities
* edge treatment
* grounding of objects
* environmental variation
* near-camera detail

Objects should feel intentionally placed rather than procedurally dumped into the world.

#

replies.author: ItsAlwaysTerminal
replies.body:
# C. MATERIALS AND TEXTURES

Audit every prominent material.

Evaluate:

* texture resolution
* texel density
* normal detail
* roughness
* metallic response
* specularity
* surface variation
* tiling visibility
* texture stretching
* UV artifacts
* overly clean surfaces
* inappropriate noise
* material scale
* edge wear where stylistically appropriate
* decals
* macro/micro detail separation
* visual consistency

Materials must communicate what objects are made from.

Metal should read as metal.

Wood should read as wood.

Stone should read as stone.

Fabric should read as fabric.

Wet surfaces should behave differently from dry ones if appropriate.

Avoid uniformly shiny or uniformly matte scenes.

# D. LIGHTING

Create a dedicated lighting pass.

Evaluate:

* key lighting
* fill
* rim/separation
* ambient illumination
* shadows
* contact shadows
* indirect lighting
* environmental lighting
* interior/exterior transitions
* dynamic range
* shadow softness
* shadow resolution
* color temperature
* light placement
* dramatic composition
* gameplay readability
* performance cost

Lighting must do more than illuminate objects.

It should establish:

* depth
* mood
* composition
* hierarchy
* atmosphere

Characters and interactive objects must remain readable.

# E. SHADOW QUALITY

Audit:

* resolution
* cascades
* acne
* peter-panning
* swimming
* popping
* contact shadow quality
* distance behavior
* temporal instability
* performance cost

Fix visibly distracting artifacts.

# F. POST-PROCESSING AND IMAGE QUALITY

Evaluate whether the game benefits from:

* tone mapping
* exposure
* bloom
* color grading
* ambient occlusion
* anti-aliasing
* sharpening
* depth of field
* motion blur
* vignette
* chromatic aberration
* volumetric effects
* atmospheric perspective

Do not blindly enable every effect.

Each effect must have a visual purpose.

Avoid the "effects soup" failure mode.

The final image should remain:

* readable
* stable
* crisp where appropriate
* aesthetically coherent

# G. PARTICLES AND VFX

Audit all gameplay events that should visually communicate:

* movement
* impacts
* collisions
* attacks
* pickups
* damage
* success
* failure
* environmental interaction
* destruction
* spawning
* disappearing
* transitions

Consider:

* particles
* sparks
* dust
* smoke
* debris
* trails
* splashes
* shockwaves
* glows
* decals
* screen-space effects
* secondary environmental reactions

Every effect must have appropriate:

* timing
* scale
* direction
* lifetime
* intensity

Effects should reinforce gameplay rather than obscure it.

# PHASE 2 — ANIMATION QUALITY

Assign a dedicated **Animation Director Agent**.

Audit every visible animated object and character.

# CHARACTER ANIMATION

Evaluate:

* idle
* walk
* run
* sprint
* jump
* falling
* landing
* turning
* stopping
* acceleration
* deceleration
* attacks
* interactions
* damage reactions
* death
* contextual actions

Check:

* pose quality
* weight
* timing
* anticipation
* follow-through
* overlapping action
* arcs
* exaggeration where appropriate
* center of gravity
* foot placement
* foot sliding
* limb penetration
* transition quality
* blend quality
* animation speed
* synchronization with movement

Movement must not feel like a model sliding through the world.

# SECONDARY MOTION

Inspect whether appropriate objects should have:

* cloth response
* hair movement
* equipment movement
* foliage response
* suspension
* body follow-through
* recoil
* procedural motion
* environmental response

Secondary motion is one of the strongest signals of polish.

Use it appropriately.

# PROCEDURAL ANIMATION / IK

Where useful, evaluate:

* foot IK
* hand IK
* look-at
* aim offsets
* terrain adaptation
* slope adaptation
* dynamic leaning
* recoil
* procedural head movement
* breathing
* idle variation

Avoid robotic motion.

# TRANSITIONS

Explicitly inspect transitions between animations.

Look for:

* snapping
* popping
* bad blends
* frozen poses
* interrupted animations
* direction-change artifacts
* incorrect blend duration

A good individual animation with bad transitions still fails.

# PHASE 3 — PHYSICS AND PHYSICAL BELIEVABILITY

Assign a dedicated **Physics / Gameplay Feel Agent**.

Audit:

* gravity
* acceleration
* inertia
* friction
* collision
* restitution
* impulses
* mass
* momentum
* object interaction
* ragdolls if applicable
* projectile behavior
* vehicle behavior if applicable
* environmental reactions

Physics should support gameplay and visual believability.

Do not assume physically accurate means fun.

Optimize for believable and satisfying behavior.

# COLLISION QUALITY

Aggressively test:

* walls
* corners
* slopes
* ledges
* stairs
* ceilings
* moving objects
* high-speed impacts
* small objects
* stacked objects
* player/world interactions

Find and eliminate:

* tunneling
* snagging
* jitter
* clipping
* explosive impulses
* floating objects
* unstable resting
* collision mismatch

# PHASE 4 — GAME FEEL

Create a dedicated **Game Feel / Juice Agent**.

Evaluate every common player action.

Ask:

>

Inspect:

* movement responsiveness
* acceleration curves
* deceleration
* jumping
* landing
* attacks
* hits
* impacts
* pickups
* buttons
* interactions
* success states
* failure states

Consider appropriately:

* hit stop
* camera impulse
* camera shake
* recoil
* squash/stretch
* particles
* animation accents
* sound synchronization
* trails
* brief flashes
* environmental reaction
* controller rumble where applicable

Do not overdo feedback.

Precision and restraint matter.

# PHASE 5 — CAMERA

Create a dedicated camera-quality pass.

Evaluate:

* framing
* lag
* smoothing
* responsiveness
* rotation
* collision
* obstruction
* field of view
* gameplay readability
* transitions
* camera shake
* zoom
* dynamic framing
* motion sickness risk

The camera should feel intentionally directed rather than merely attached to the player.

Test stressful gameplay situations.

# PHASE 6 — ENVIRONMENTAL LIFE

Static environments often make otherwise competent games feel cheap.

Audit opportunities for appropriate ambient motion:

* foliage
* dust
* smoke
* clouds
* water
* reflections
* lights
* machinery
* signage
* animals
* insects
* distant movement
* environmental particles
* atmospheric effects

Do not add motion everywhere.

Use it strategically to prevent environments from feeling dead.

# PHASE 7 — UI / HUD VISUAL QUALITY

If the game contains UI, assign a dedicated UI reviewer.

Evaluate:

* typography
* hierarchy
* spacing
* alignment
* icon quality
* visual consistency
* readability
* animation
* transitions
* hover states
* pressed states
* disabled states
* information density
* scaling
* resolution independence

Remove default browser/framework/programmer styling unless intentionally part of the design.

UI animation should be fast, purposeful, and polished.

# PHASE 8 — MICRO-POLISH

Once major systems are good, perform a dedicated micro-polish pass.

Look specifically for small defects that collectively make games feel unfinished:

* abrupt transitions
* repeated textures
* visible seams
* inconsistent shadows
* clipping
* floating props
* missing particles
* missing impact reactions
* abrupt object disappearance
* animation pops
* UI inconsistencies
* poor cursor states
* wrong scale
* awkward camera clipping
* inconsistent easing
* missing environmental motion
* overly sterile surfaces
* excessive bloom
* excessive saturation
* poor contrast
* visual noise
* z-fighting
* flickering
* temporal instability
* texture stretching
* aliasing
* poor transparency sorting

Treat these as real defects.

#

replies.author: ItsAlwaysTerminal
replies.body:
# SPECIALIST AGENT STRUCTURE

Fan out specialist agents whenever supported.

Suggested roles:

# Agent 1 — Art Director

Owns overall visual coherence.

# Agent 2 — Environment / Asset Artist

Owns geometry, props, environmental detail, scale, composition.

# Agent 3 — Material / Shader Specialist

Owns materials, textures, shaders, surface response.

# Agent 4 — Lighting Artist

Owns lighting, shadows, atmosphere, exposure.

# Agent 5 — VFX Artist

Owns particles and effects.

# Agent 6 — Animation Director

Owns character/object animation and transitions.

# Agent 7 — Physics Specialist

Owns physical behavior and collision.

# Agent 8 — Gameplay Feel Specialist

Owns responsiveness, impact, juice, and action feedback.

# Agent 9 — Camera Specialist

Owns camera presentation and behavior.

# Agent 10 — UI / Motion Design Specialist

Owns HUD/UI presentation where applicable.

# Agent 11 — Performance Engineer

Owns FPS, frame time, memory, shader cost, draw calls, loading behavior, and regressions.

# Agent 12 — Visual QA / Adversarial Critic

Does NOT implement first-pass work.

Its primary responsibility is finding reasons to reject the other agents' work.

Create additional specialist agents when the project reveals domains not covered here.

# ADVERSARIAL REVIEW PROTOCOL

Every major visual subsystem must be reviewed by an agent that did NOT implement it.

The review agent should behave like an unusually demanding:

* AAA art director,
* technical artist,
* animation director,
* graphics engineer,
* or gameplay polish reviewer,

depending on the subsystem.

The critic's job is NOT to congratulate the implementation agent.

The critic's job is to find defects.

Require the critic to explicitly provide:

1. strongest qualities,
2. weakest qualities,
3. visible defects,
4. technical concerns,
5. inconsistencies,
6. highest-value improvements,
7. severity ranking,
8. pass/fail decision.

# VISUAL EVIDENCE IS REQUIRED

Do not approve visual work from code inspection alone.

Where tooling permits, capture screenshots or short videos showing:

* before
* after
* important gameplay states
* multiple camera angles
* movement
* transitions
* effects

Review the rendered result.

If automated vision is available, use it.

If browser screenshots are available, use them.

If video-frame inspection is available, use it.

Runtime appearance is the source of truth.

# CONTROLLED A/B COMPARISON

For major visual changes, perform controlled comparison.

Use:

* identical scene
* identical camera
* identical resolution
* identical gameplay state
* identical environmental conditions when practical

Compare Candidate A and Candidate B without allowing the evaluator to be biased by implementation history when the harness permits blinded comparison.

The reviewer should score both independently.

Suggested categories:

|Category|Score|
|:-|:-|
|Overall visual quality|/10|
|Composition|/10|
|Material quality|/10|
|Lighting|/10|
|Depth|/10|
|Animation quality|/10|
|Physical believability|/10|
|Gameplay readability|/10|
|Art-direction consistency|/10|
|Professional polish|/10|
|Visual defects|penalty|
|Performance regressions|penalty|

The reviewer must explain WHY one candidate is superior.

Do not accept "A looks better."

Require concrete observations.

# REFERENCE-QUALITY COMPARISON

Where legally and technically appropriate, use high-quality commercial games or professional artwork as **quality references**, not assets to copy.

Compare qualities such as:

* lighting sophistication
* material response
* environmental density
* silhouette
* animation fluidity
* composition
* VFX timing
* camera behavior
* readability
* polish

Do not duplicate copyrighted assets or distinctive designs.

The purpose is to establish a professional quality bar.

# QUALITY SCORECARD

Maintain a scorecard throughout the project.

Score every major category from 0–10:

* art direction
* environment
* geometry
* materials
* textures
* lighting
* shadows
* image quality
* VFX
* animation
* secondary motion
* physics
* collision
* game feel
* camera
* UI
* environmental life
* polish
* stability
* performance

Interpretation:

**0–3:** prototype quality  
**4–5:** visibly unfinished  
**6:** competent indie quality  
**7:** professional  
**8:** highly polished  
**9:** exceptional  
**10:** extraordinarily difficult to materially improve

Do not inflate scores.

An 8 should mean genuinely impressive.

A 9 should be rare.

A 10 should be extremely rare.

# ITERATION LOOP

For EACH subsystem:

1. inspect current state,
2. document defects,
3. establish intended result,
4. implement improvements,
5. run the game,
6. capture visual/runtime evidence,
7. perform technical checks,
8. send output to independent critic,
9. receive criticism,
10. rank criticism by impact,
11. repair legitimate weaknesses,
12. capture new evidence,
13. compare against previous version,
14. re-review,
15. repeat while high-value improvements remain.

Use `/loop` or equivalent autonomous iteration mechanisms where available.

Do not loop blindly.

Each iteration must have:

* a hypothesis,
* a concrete modification,
* an evaluation,
* a decision.

# STOPPING RULE

Do NOT use:

>

That is subjective and potentially infinite.

Instead, a subsystem may terminate only when ALL of these are true:

# Functional gate

No known material gameplay defect.

# Visual gate

No obvious placeholder-quality or visibly unfinished element remains.

# Technical gate

No known critical technical defect.

# Performance gate

Performance remains within the defined target.

# Regression gate

Previously functioning systems remain functional.

# Critic gate

Independent critic gives PASS.

# Score gate

No quality category relevant to the subsystem is below **8/10**, unless there is a documented technical or asset limitation preventing it.

# Diminishing-returns gate

The critic cannot identify another reasonable change expected to create a meaningful player-visible improvement without disproportionately harming performance, maintainability, scope, or art-direction coherence.

This is the termination condition.

#

replies.author: ItsAlwaysTerminal
replies.body:
# PERFORMANCE IS PART OF VISUAL QUALITY

Do not "improve" graphics by destroying performance.

Establish an explicit performance target from the project's likely deployment environment.

If none exists, infer a reasonable target and document the assumption.

Profile:

* average FPS
* 1% low FPS where measurable
* frame-time stability
* CPU cost
* GPU cost
* memory
* texture memory
* shader complexity
* draw calls
* object count
* particles
* loading
* garbage collection / allocation spikes

Any major visual enhancement must be checked for performance regression.

Prefer clever quality over brute-force cost.

# DO NOT DAMAGE THE CODEBASE FOR VISUAL POLISH

Maintain clean engineering standards.

Avoid:

* massive monolithic files
* duplicated systems
* hard-coded scene hacks
* unmaintainable shaders
* undocumented magic constants
* unnecessary dependencies
* global-state abuse
* fragile timing hacks

If existing architectural problems directly prevent quality improvements, refactor them deliberately.

Do not perform unrelated rewrites.

# SOURCE-CONTROL DISCIPLINE

Work incrementally.

Before risky changes:

* inspect repository status,
* understand existing changes,
* avoid destroying unrelated work.

Create logical checkpoints where tooling permits.

Do not overwrite work from another sub-agent.

Coordinate file ownership when agents run concurrently.

# REGRESSION TESTING

After every substantial batch of improvements, test:

* startup
* loading
* player movement
* collisions
* primary mechanics
* camera
* UI
* important interactions
* major effects
* animation states
* level transitions
* restart/death states
* performance

If automated tests exist, run them.

Add useful tests where practical.

Visual polish does not justify regressions.

# CRITIC BEHAVIOR

The visual critic must be intentionally skeptical.

Use instructions equivalent to:

>

However, the critic must remain technically rational.

Do not invent defects simply to continue looping.

# FINAL DIRECTOR PASS

After all specialist agents report completion, perform a completely fresh top-to-bottom inspection as Executive Director.

Assume you have never seen the project before.

Play through representative gameplay.

Ask:

* What immediately looks weak?
* What feels cheap?
* What looks generic?
* What breaks immersion?
* What is inconsistent?
* What does not move naturally?
* What lacks feedback?
* Where does the eye go?
* Is that where the eye SHOULD go?
* Are important objects readable?
* Are materials believable?
* Does lighting have intent?
* Does animation communicate weight?
* Does physics feel coherent?
* Does the world feel alive?
* Does the camera help presentation?
* Does anything still feel like a prototype?
* Are there frame-rate problems?
* Are there temporal artifacts?
* Are there visual bugs?
* Would a professional reviewer immediately notice unfinished areas?

Generate a **Final Punch List**.

Fan the punch-list items back out to appropriate specialist agents.

Repeat review and correction until the remaining items meet the stopping rule.

# FINAL DELIVERABLE

When the work is complete, produce a final report containing:

# 1. Executive Summary

Explain the overall transformation.

# 2. Major Improvements

Describe the most consequential improvements made.

# 3. Visual Systems

Summarize:

* art direction
* geometry
* materials
* textures
* lighting
* shadows
* post-processing
* VFX
* environmental presentation

# 4. Motion

Summarize:

* animation
* transitions
* procedural animation
* secondary motion

# 5. Gameplay Presentation

Summarize:

* physics
* game feel
* camera
* feedback

# 6. UI

Summarize UI improvements where applicable.

# 7. Performance

Provide before/after performance information where measurable.

# 8. Bugs / Regressions

List defects discovered and fixed.

# 9. Remaining Limitations

Explicitly identify anything preventing higher quality, such as:

* insufficient source assets
* engine limitations
* missing animation data
* hardware limitations
* unavailable art resources

Do not hide limitations.

# 10. Quality Scorecard

Provide final 0–10 scores for every applicable category.

# 11. Verification Evidence

List screenshots, videos, test runs, benchmarks, and comparison artifacts used during review.

# IMPORTANT AUTONOMY RULES

You have broad authority to make reasonable improvements needed to accomplish the mission.

Do not continually ask the user for permission for ordinary implementation decisions.

Infer reasonable choices from:

* the existing game
* existing art direction
* repository structure
* established gameplay
* platform constraints

When an issue can be solved through inspection, experimentation, benchmarking, or specialist review, solve it rather than asking the user.

Only preserve ambiguity when choosing incorrectly would fundamentally change the intended game.

# ABSOLUTE FAILURE CONDITIONS

The mission is NOT complete if any prominent area still has:

* obvious placeholder graphics
* obviously weak animation
* floating/sliding motion
* visibly broken collision
* severe clipping
* bad texture stretching
* visually distracting seams
* glaring lighting artifacts
* obvious material inconsistencies
* excessive effect spam
* major aliasing/flicker
* severe frame pacing issues
* visibly dead environments where motion is expected
* weak or missing gameplay feedback
* unfinished UI
* major performance regression
* broken gameplay caused by visual improvements

# PRIMARY DIRECTIVE

Do not optimize for the quantity of changes.

Do not optimize for the number of sub-agents.

Do not optimize for how impressive the change log sounds.

Optimize for the **actual player-visible result**.

Every implementation decision should answer:

>

Use specialist parallelism, adversarial review, visual inspection, controlled comparisons, profiling, and repeated iteration to push each important subsystem toward exceptional professional quality.

The final product—not the effort expended—is the metric.

replies.author: iClickHereAndThere
replies.body:
This is so true.

I literally just use free Chat-GPT and the fastest dumbest model.. 

I was new to game dev and ai and on and off different projects over the last year I've learned so much. At the beginning I was just asking AI if something is possible, giving it documentation for the coding language I was using and telling it to walk me through creating something like it was speaking to a 5 year old. 

It was always messing up and fast. Obviously. 

But then I started asking for explanations, doing my own research on industries standards and practices, supplying this information to the AI, learning the names of properties and syntax and what and when to use them.

Over time, I just feel like I actually started to understand what a script may be used for, how it works, where I can change things to get my desired results if it isn't exactly what I was looking for. 

The more I knew and could specify exactly what I needed, wanted, offer potential solutions ahead of time, have the ai compare which is best, explain why and make the final decisions for myself and my use case, the shit really spits out very close to what I need and am looking for in these cases. 

NOW, I'm at this weird crossroad where I still feel like I should learn to create and implement code myself to really solidify and learn this information and make using AI even more reliable and efficient or if what I'm doing now is enough

replies.author: Atmic
replies.body:
If you're using Claude Code, use Claude Desktop in a separate window and create a project folder in there where you're working on the app/game. 

Designate the Claude Desktop role as the organizer and prompt creator, and discuss what you want to do next with it: it creates the prompts in detail for Claude Code to implement. 

One step further, in Claude Code use the novel OpusPlan and paste the Claude Desktop prompt in plan mode, then switch to auto to implement it in Sonnet.

If you're using OpenAI, adjust this workflow for GPT Desktop and Codex respectively. 

You stay in complete control and the prompts will be immaculate for every step.
